extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing claim-drafting/examination guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on determining whether claim language meets definiteness and related claim-drafting requirements (antecedent basis, functional language, alternative/negative limitations, multiplicity, etc.). Covers when to reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph and related support/enablement/written-description considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary Claim Language ("for example," "such as")
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of examples or preferences is properly set forth in the specification rather than the claims. If stated in the claims, examples and preferences may lead to confusion over the intended scope of a claim. Note that the mere use of the phrase "such as" or "for example" in a claim does not by itself render the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is not clear whether the claimed narrower range is a limitation, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph should be made. The examiner should analyze whether the metes and bounds of the claim are clearly set forth. Examples held indefinite (fact specific): (A) “R is halogen, for example, chlorine”; (B) “material such as rock wool or asbestos”; (C) “lighter hydrocarbons, such, for example, as the vapors or gas produced”; (D) “normal operating conditions such as while in the container of a proportioner”; (E) “coke, brick, or like material”. The above examples are fact specific and should not be applied as per se rules. See MPEP § 2173.02 for guidance regarding when it is appropriate to make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Antecedent Basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear (e.g., use of "said lever" or "the lever" without prior recitation). Lack of antecedent basis can make it unclear which element is referenced and thus render the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether a term has been given reasonable antecedent basis; failure to provide explicit antecedent basis does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable by those skilled in the art (e.g., "controlled stream of fluid" provided antecedent basis for "the controlled fluid"). Inherent components of elements have antecedent basis in the recitation of the elements themselves (e.g., "the outer surface of said sphere"). I. Examiner should suggest corrections to antecedent problems — many are drafting oversights easily corrected and examiner should act constructively. II. A claim term with no antecedent in the disclosure is not necessarily indefinite; applicants have latitude in wording so long as terms define the invention with reasonable clarity. III. A claim is not per se indefinite if the body recites additional elements not in the preamble; totality of limitations must be considered (see In re Larsen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Limitations in Another Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim which makes reference to a preceding claim to define a limitation is an acceptable claim construction and should not necessarily be rejected as improper or confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of acceptable formats: “The product produced by the method of claim 1.” or “A method of producing ethanol comprising contacting amylose with the culture of claim 1 under the following conditions .....” Such references are not inherently indefinite (see Ex parte Porter). However, where the format of making reference to limitations recited in another claim results in confusion, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is proper. When examining dependent claims, determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (pre‑AIA 112, fourth paragraph). See MPEP § 608.01(n), subsection III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term is functional when it recites a feature 'by what it does rather than by what it is'. Functional language is not inherently improper; 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA sixth paragraph) expressly authorizes means/step‑plus‑function claiming, and functional language can be used outside means‑plus‑function format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate functional limitations for what they fairly convey to a person of ordinary skill in the art in context. Functional claiming often includes some structure followed by its function (e.g., conical spout that 'allow[ed] several kernels... to pass through'). Permissible examples: limitations defining radicals by what they cannot do, 'members adapted to be positioned', etc. Problems arise when claims merely state a problem solved or a result achieved (e.g., "aesthetically pleasing" screen) because boundaries of scope may be unclear. Unlimited functional limitations that encompass all means of resolving a problem may not be supported by the written description or be commensurate in scope with enabling disclosure (see Ariad, Hyatt). Factors examiners should consider when functional language is used: (1) whether there is a clear‑cut indication of scope; (2) whether well‑defined boundaries exist or the claim only states a problem/result; (3) whether a person of ordinary skill would know what structure or steps are encompassed. These factors are illustrative, not exhaustive; other art‑specific factors may apply. During prosecution, ambiguities can be resolved by applicant through: (1) using a quantitative metric (numeric limitation) rather than qualitative functional feature; (2) providing a formula and examples that meet/do not meet the limitation; (3) providing general guideline and examples sufficient to teach a skilled person when the limitation is satisfied; or (4) amending claims to recite particular structure that accomplishes the function. Examiners should remember that definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is distinct from written description/enablement issues under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush Groups (Alternative Limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a list of alternatives to define a limitation (Markush grouping) is an acceptable construction and should not necessarily be rejected as confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). A Markush grouping is typically a closed group of alternatives (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatment is not governed by particular format (e.g., 'consisting of' vs 'A, B, or C'). If a Markush grouping uses an open list (e.g., 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of'), the claim should generally be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended. If combinations/mixtures of alternatives are intended, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member selected from the group' or 'or mixtures thereof'). A Markush group may be large and broad without being indefinite (breadth is not indefiniteness), but if so expansive that skilled artisans cannot determine metes and bounds, an indefiniteness rejection is appropriate. Use of Markush claims of diminishing scope is not by itself objectionable, but if it renders claims indefinite or causes undue multiplicity, reject appropriately. Double inclusion of an element in a Markush group is not per se a basis for rejection — evaluate facts to see if redundancy renders the claim indefinite (examples and case law cited, e.g., Eli Lilly v. Teva). See MPEP § 2117 and § 803.02 and Supplementary Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Optionally' in Alternative Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the term 'optionally' in listing alternatives can be acceptable where there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Cordova and Ex parte Wu held language like 'containing A, B, and optionally C' acceptable because no ambiguity existed as to covered alternatives. If the list of potential alternatives can vary and ambiguity arises, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is proper and the examiner should explain the confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative limitations (defining what an invention is not) are not inherently ambiguous if the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely, albeit negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older cases criticized negative limitations as claiming by exclusion, but modern view accepts them if definite (examples: excluding proteins/soaps/resins/sugars from a homopolymer). Any negative limitation or exclusionary proviso must have basis in the original disclosure. If alternatives are positively recited in the specification, they may be explicitly excluded in the claims. Mere absence of a positive recitation is not necessarily a basis for exclusion; however, lack of literal basis for a negative limitation may not establish a prima facie lack of descriptive support — the disclosure must 'reasonably convey[] to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession' of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date. While silence will not generally suffice to support a negative limitation, in some circumstances a skilled artisan would understand a negative limitation to necessarily be present. Any claim containing a negative limitation lacking basis in the original disclosure should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph) for failing the written description requirement. See MPEP § 2163 - § 2163.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Old Combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'old combination'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the 1952 Patent Act, courts/Board have taken the view that an 'old combination' rejection is no longer valid. Claims should be considered proper so long as they comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b). The old principle (Lincoln Engineering) required citation of a single reference broadly disclosing a combination functionally cooperating to produce substantially the same results; subsequent case law (Bernhart, Radio Steel) and Board decisions have effectively legislated that principle out. Accordingly, do not reject claims merely because they are an old combination if they meet statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Gustafson, In re Collier) indicates 'aggregation' is a non‑statutory rejection and should not be used. If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by the specification, see MPEP § 2172.01 for treatment. Assess whether the rejection is actually under a statutory ground (101/102/103/112) rather than a non‑statutory 'aggregation' label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolix
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are overly long or contain unimportant details should be rejected as prolix only when such recitations render the scope of the claimed invention indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject as prolix when long recitations prevent determination of the metes and bounds of the claimed subject matter. The basis for prolix rejection is that the long/irrelevant recitations cause indefiniteness — do not use prolix to penalize mere length if scope remains ascertainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity (Undue Multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one claim may be presented provided they differ substantially from each other and are not unduly multiplied (37 CFR 1.75). Where applicant presents an unreasonable number of repetitious/multiplied claims that confuse rather than clarify, an undue multiplicity rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the rule of reason on a case‑by‑case basis; undue multiplicity rejections should be rare and applied judiciously (see In re Chandler, In re Flint). If appropriate, examiner should contact applicant by telephone to explain undue multiplicity and request selection of a specified number of claims for examination. If applicant selects claims, make undue multiplicity rejection on remaining claims in next Office action and proceed on merits with selected claims. If applicant refuses selection, make undue multiplicity rejection of all claims in next action. Applicant's reply must include selection of claims no greater than number specified by examiner; if the rejection is adhered to, repeat it and examine selected claims on the merits. This preserves applicant's right to review by PTAB. It is possible to reject one claim over an allowed claim if they differ only by subject matter old in the art (Ex parte Whitelaw doctrine), but that doctrine is restricted to unduly multiplied or substantial duplicates (see Ex parte Kochan).
